passages.t: The watchman, and a people asking how to live
passages.happening:
God repeats the case of the watchman. If a watchman sees the sword coming and blows the horn, those who ignore it are responsible for their own deaths. ‘But if the watchman sees the sword coming and fails to blow the horn to warn the people’, God will hold the watchman accountable (verse 6). ‘As for you, O son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel’ (verse 7).

The people are saying, ‘Our transgressions and our sins are heavy upon us, and we are wasting away because of them’ (verse 10). How can they live? God answers, ‘As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live’ (verse 11). A righteous person cannot trust in past righteousness while doing wrong, and a wicked person who turns and makes restitution will live (verses 12-16). The people say God's way is not fair; he answers that he judges each by his ways (verses 17-20).
passages.hearers:
Cities posted watchmen on walls and towers to see danger early and sound the ram's horn, so the people could take refuge or prepare to fight. God uses that familiar office to define the prophet's duty, repeating his charge from chapter 3 at the turning point of the book.

The people's cry in verse 10 is new. Before, they denied their guilt. Now they are crushed by it. God's answer is not to deny their sin but to call them to turn and live.
passages.later: The people's despair recalls the lament, ‘Our fathers sinned and are no more’ (Lamentations 5:7). Isaiah too called, ‘Turn to Me and be saved’ (Isaiah 45:22).
passages.hard:
Is God really fair if one sin can cancel a lifetime of righteousness, and one turn can cancel a lifetime of wickedness?

The exiles raised this very objection (verses 17 and 20). The passage seems to judge a person by their last direction rather than by a total. Interpreters answer in a few ways. Many note that Ezekiel is not describing a single slip but a settled turn, a righteous person who trusts in his own record and then makes wrongdoing a way of life (verse 13). Others stress that the passage is pastoral before it is systematic: it is spoken to people crushed by guilt (verse 10), to tell them the past need not decide their future, and to people who presumed on their past, to tell them it cannot protect them.

Christian traditions differ on what this means for whether believers can fall away. Reformed readers usually take the warnings as a real means by which God keeps his people; Wesleyan and Arminian readers take them as showing that a believer can truly fall away. This site takes no side. On any reading, God is not keeping a ledger to trap anyone; he is calling everyone to turn and live.
passages.asks: The people said their sins were heavy and asked how they could live. Ask what guilt you are carrying that feels too heavy. And ask what it would mean to believe that God wants you to live.

passages.happening:
In the twelfth year of the exile, on the fifth day of the tenth month, a fugitive from Jerusalem came to Ezekiel and reported, “The city has been taken!” (verse 21). The evening before, God had opened Ezekiel's mouth, and he was no longer mute (verse 22).

Those living in the ruins of the land say, ‘Abraham was only one man, yet he possessed the land. But we are many’ (verse 24). God answers that they eat meat with the blood, worship idols, shed blood and defile their neighbors' wives; will they possess the land? (verses 25-26). It will be made desolate (verses 27-29).

The exiles talk about Ezekiel by the walls and in doorways and come to hear him, ‘but they do not put them into practice’ (verse 31). ‘Indeed, you are to them like a singer of love songs with a beautiful voice, who skillfully plays an instrument’ (verse 32). When it all comes to pass, they will know that a prophet has been among them (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
The news came about January 585 BC on the most common reckoning. Babylon had breached the walls in the summer, and the temple was burned about a month later. If the city fell in 586 BC, the news took about five months, a reasonable time for the road from Judah to Babylonia; scholars who date the fall to 587 BC count Ezekiel's years differently or follow a reading of eleventh year.

Babylon left the poorest people behind to work the fields, and after the murder of the governor Gedaliah conditions there were chaotic. Some who remained saw themselves as the rightful heirs. They turned Abraham's story into a title deed; God answers that the land was never held apart from faithfulness.

The last verses show the prophet as a local celebrity, discussed and enjoyed like a performer, and not obeyed.
passages.later: Babylon ‘left behind some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and fields’ (2 Kings 25:12). Isaiah said, ‘When I called him, he was but one’ (Isaiah 51:2).
passages.asks: The exiles enjoyed Ezekiel's words like a beautiful song and did nothing about them. Ask whether you listen to sermons or read Scripture as entertainment. And ask what one thing you have heard that you need to put into practice.
